platform: native Windows x64; actual filesystem, Git Bash processes and loopback HTTP gateway; no remote provider
changes: All worker handler/stop/backstop responses supply a trusted consumeRequestPath fence to both built-in queue clients.

Under the existing real response mutex, prepare all response bytes, atomically rename the request to a non-JSON .paperclip-delivery-unknown claim, then publish. Delete the claim only after publication. Failed publication or claim cleanup retains the unknown claim; late unconditional writers cannot republish it.
A missing/unreadable lock PID is not stale proof. The filesystem client waits, matching the command client, and reaps only a valid PID proven absent with ESRCH.

Replace elapsed handler/cleanup sleeps with actual handler entry, held remote mutex, competing late writer, real HTTP consumption, and completed response-command gates. Two stops enumerate concurrently; out-of-lock request cleanup is deliberately held until the late writer finishes.

limits: This proves the tested live-process concurrency and explicit IO failure boundaries, not a two-file power-loss transaction or globally exactly-once host mutations.

Unknown claims are retained in responses with a non-JSON suffix. Built-in pending-request enumerators never list them, and ordinary shutdown/remove only targets the original request; no automatic restoration/replay is added.

Claim failure before rename may retry publication; claim/publication uncertainty after the rename fails closed. The existing gateway classifies a dispatched unsafe missing receipt as 409 indeterminate; that mapping is retained, not newly claimed as a separately injected end-to-end HTTP fault test.
The optional consume fence is implemented and verified by the two shipped built-in clients. Older third-party clients that ignore the new option are not qualified by this receipt.
Negative-path tests deliberately emit expected fault diagnostics; the complete suite has zero failed tests. No secrets or real user data are contained in this receipt.
